sections.normalized_html:
This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression:

[MATH: (x^{2} + 2)/(x^{2} + 1)|= (x^{2} + 1 + 1)/(x^{2} + 1); = (x^{2} + 1)/(x^{2} + 1) + (1)/(x^{2} + 1); = 1 + (1)/(x^{2} + 1).]

Remembering that [MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \textrm dx = \arctan(x),]

we can now calculate the integral and get [MATH: ∫(x^{2} + 2)/(x^{2} + 1)dx|= ∫(1 + (1)/(x^{2} + 1))dx; = ∫1dx + ∫(1)/(x^{2} + 1)dx; = x + \arctan (x) + C.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall the following derivatives of the inverse trigonometric functions:

Content:
[MATH: (d)/(dx)(\arcsin x)|= (1)/(sqrt(1 − x^{2})); (d)/(dx)(\arctan x)|= (1)/(1 + x^{2}); (d)/(dx)(arcsecx)|= (1)/(|x|sqrt(x^{2} − 1))]

Content:
Since integration is the opposite of differentiation, we arrive at the following results:
[MATH: ∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − x^{2}))dx|= \arcsin (x) + C; ∫(1)/(1 + x^{2})dx|= \arctan (x) + C; ∫(1)/(|x|sqrt(x^{2} − 1))dx|= arcsec(x) + C]

---

Therefore, we have

Item 11 — Example: Integrating Using Inverse Trigonometric Functions and Some Manipulations

Example Prompt:
Evaluate the integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int \dfrac {x^2+2}{x^2 + 1}\, \textrm{d}x.]

Explanation:

Remembering that
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \textrm dx = \arctan(x),]

we can now calculate the integral and get
[MATH: ∫(x^{2} + 2)/(x^{2} + 1)dx|= ∫(1 + (1)/(x^{2} + 1))dx; = ∫1dx + ∫(1)/(x^{2} + 1)dx; = x + \arctan (x) + C.]
